title: How High Expectations Can Improve Performance
paragraphs: What we expect of people influences how we treat them, and how we treat them influences their behavior.
Psychologists call this phenomenon the Pygmalion effect, after an old story told by the Roman poet Ovid.
A sculptor, called Pygmalion, created a statue of a woman so beautiful he fell in love with it. Pygmalion prayed for a wife as beautiful as his statue — and his statue came to life!

Then, in 1912, the Irish writer George Bernard Shaw wrote a play called Pygmalion about a professor who teaches a working-class girl how to speak like a lady. In the play, the girl says what makes someone a lady is "not how she behaves, but how she's treated."
In 1968, the psychologist Robert Rosenthal and the elementary school principal Lenore Jacobson published a book called Pygmalion in the Classroom.

The book describes an experiment in which Rosenthal's research team gave students at Jacobson's school a test. Without showing the results, the researchers told the teachers that some students had more academic potential.
Those students were actually chosen at random. But in a test given later in the year, the results of those randomly chosen students improved the most.

Rosenthal suggested the teachers' higher expectations for those students caused them to treat the children differently — perhaps by paying them more attention — and this influenced the students' performance.

So this is the Pygmalion effect: when we have high expectations for people, they are likely to perform better and make those expectations come true. However, if we have low expectations for people, they are just as likely to perform poorly.

We may not realize we are treating people differently, and this treatment might not be obvious — it could be just a mood or a look. But it is important for leaders — whether teachers, parents or managers — to think about how their expectations can encourage people to do better.
